newsitem.title: USA: FCC proposes tougher phone rules against "slamming".
newsitem.headline: FCC proposes tougher phone rules against "slamming".

text.p: Flooded with thousands of complaints, federal regulators Tuesday proposed to beef up rules that protect consumers from having their phone service switched without their approval.
The Federal Communications Commission proposed to extend its rules against "slamming" to unapproved changes in local phone service -- on top of existing rules overing long-distance calling.
The plan would tighten company procedures for verifying changes in a customer's local and long-distance service.
The proposal also would make unauthorised phone companies liable for perks, such as frequent-flier miles, that "slammed" consumers would have received from their regular carrier.
And the FCC is considering whether to require consumers to continue paying unauthorised carriers for phone service.
Consumers must now pay the new carrier at a rate equal to the amount that the authorised company would have charged for the calls.
"The measures we are proposing aim to ensure that slamming does not pay -- and will make it harder for consumers to be slammed in the first place," Commissioner Susan Ness said.
With this proposal, "we are shutting the door on slamming," she added.

The plan would beef up rules adopted in 1995 and would put into effect portions of last year's big communications act, which is designed to get the local and long-distance phone companies into each other's business.
Prior to the new law, slamming was confined primarily to the long-distance business.
"Slamming is definitely something we see as a bigger problem as competition comes to the local phone market," said Cleo Manuel of the National Consumers League, an advocacy group.
The FCC receives more complaints about slamming than any other phone-related complaint. Last year, the agency logged some 16,000 complaints, up from about 11,000 in 1995.
Phone customers changed long-distance carriers 50 million times last year.
The FCC has found that smaller companies using outside sales forces garnered more complaints than well-established companies such as long-distance giant AT&T Corp..
Over the past two years, the FCC has taken action against 15 companies, meting out more than $1 million in penalties.
Among the types of schemes cited: consumers unknowingly signing up for a new carrier by entering a sweepstakes, or customers having their service switched through a phony signature on a document.

Among other things, the FCC is considering whether to bar carriers from using a "welcome package" mailed to a consumer as a method for verifying a switch in service. Consumers can unwittingly throw out such a mailing, and have their phone service changed as a result.
The agency also will study whether to require opposing phone companies in a slamming dispute to try to negotiate a settlement before asking the agency to resolve the matter.
